title: Honey, Wax, and the Shell
english: I suffer pains until Christ is formed in you. They do not become outside of the belly; they are not orphaned. Moreover, 'has my heart become like melting wax?' (Psalm 51:7). I said that what is said about it according to the human might be said also about everything righteous. His heart, when it is not light, but has something material mixed in, melts. But toward the beautiful, the melting happens; for the melting wax does not become outside of the one having it. 'In the midst' therefore 'of my belly.'

Concerning the intelligible, different names signify the same thing. I call the sheep an intelligible thing which is under the true Shepherd. This sheep is also called light in another way. Indeed, having once been asked by a philosopher whether I have something to say from the Scripture that the soul is incorporeal, I said these things: every name of a body signifies only that alone by which it is called. For example, the sensible vine is nothing other than a vine, and the stone which is so named bodily is nothing other than a stone. But when many dissimilar things are spoken of concerning the same essence, it is evident that that essence is an intelligible one. So also we speak concerning God that He is incorporeal, since He is also named light and fire and spirit and spring. These things cannot be anything bodily, but according to an intention. And such intentions concern the intelligible.

If, therefore, the man or the soul is called light, and is also called a sheep and a plant—for it is indeed called both a plant and a sheep—it cannot bodily be all these things, so that it is an intelligible essence. If, therefore, you hear [it spoken] concerning the soul, you hear [it spoken] concerning a heart, an intellect, a belly, a spring; and for it is indeed called both a plant and a sheep, do not take it according to sensation. The vessel, therefore, of the soul, in which it receives spiritual nourishments, is called a belly. Furthermore, since it is also generative, one possesses this belly both as receiving nourishments and as giving birth. You know that the wax is a follower of the honey. The composition of the honey existed previously, and because of the honey [there is] the wax, not because of the wax [there is] the honey. And just as regarding a plant, the fruit is not because of the leaf, but the leaf is because of the fruit—for it is a protector of the fruit—so the wax is not something preceding, but a follower. If, therefore, the soul...

If it possesses the preceding virtues, it is honey. But if, along with those, it has something of matter mixed in, it is wax. For this reason, he says that the sinners melt like wax 'from the presence of fire'. Honey, however, is praiseworthy; it is a preceding substance, and it signifies sweetness. Just as to sweeten is to have a healing quality. Therefore, the 35 preceding things of the soul—which are good both in movements and in activities—resemble honey; but the second things, having something of the sensible and material mixed in, are wax.

Thus a man sometimes melts; the material sometimes falls away from the intellect and the heart, so that the mind no longer has anything entangled with it, but is entirely incorporeal, just as it surpassed the beginning. 'My strength has dried up like a shell' (Ps 101:7). My strength has cast off all moisture and all liquidity, as if it had been thrown aside like a shell. And it can be said otherwise: that which is muddy in us—and you know what that is—if it remains mud, it is dissolved by the passing of moisture. But when it takes on dryness and casts off all the moisture from without from the matter, it dries up according to the shell.

Each of the examples taken is taken according to something. This is often said; for if it were taken from everything, it would not be an example, but that very thing which we wish to show. Therefore, the shell is often mocked in this way: a vessel made of shell, if broken, they say, does not receive [liquid], nor can it be glued. I say in another way: that which is made from clay, when it is hardened by fire and a kiln, casts off the soft and the easily broken. Thus 'my strength' 'has dried up like a shell'. We take it in both ways: it no longer has any moisture, nor a muddy state. It can also be taken otherwise: it has cast off all bitterness from the much approaching affliction.

'And my tongue is stuck to my jaws' (Ps 118:13). It is the custom of Scripture to speak of the sticking of the tongue to the throat to mean silence. Since my sweet things are no longer present, and since those concerning me and my listeners are no longer present, lest I seem to carry the word in vain, I have been silent: 'my tongue is stuck to my throat'. But it is not stuck when we are conversing. Through the movement of the tongue, the word is carried forth. But when it is stuck to the throat, it is silence.
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Body of Death and the Nature of Christ
english: But this silence does not come from the one being silent, but from those who are not succeeding as listeners. For he says in one of the prophets in Amos: 'Many are the fallen in every place, I will cast down silence' (Amos 8:11). If they flee, I cast down silence, so that I may not be honored to bring forth the teaching. And this indeed is one of the aids.

For instance, in Isaiah, he commands the clouds not to pour rain when the vine bears thorns instead of grapes, when, having remained [unfruitful] of the one watering in order to make righteousness, he makes iniquity. The grape is righteousness, and iniquity is the thorn. And since, being watered, he has not produced suitable fruits, but anxieties and worldly pleasures, he no longer speaks; for most often the wicked rub themselves against the words concerning virtue, learning to despise them. Sometimes, indeed, he endures the rain. And the rain and the voice mean the same thing here; for it reveals the divine teaching. Just as it no longer rains when good fruits are not being borne, so he no longer speaks nor converses when those listening have [thoughts] concerning other things. And this he speaks to men.

According to the intention of the teacher, the listeners are called disciples, but when he is the shepherd, they are sheep. And since they are no longer sheep nor men, but have become scorpions according to that which was said: 'Son of man, in the midst of scorpions you dwell' (Ezekiel 2:6). 'Many' therefore [is] 'the fallen in every place, I will cast down silence.' But it is read differently; for the wording is ambiguous. It is possible to take it thus: 'Many is the fallen in every place; I will cast down silence'; in every degree; for here the place signifies the degree, as also in others. Concerning Judas, indeed, it is said that he strayed from the place of the ministry which was entrusted to him. 'Many' therefore [is] 'the fallen in every place.' In every rank of those owing to be sober and vigilant and to speak of the things of virtue, 'the fallen is many,' except not all. 'I will cast down silence.' And it is possible also to divide the verse thus: 'Many is the fallen. In every place I will cast down silence.'

I do not only keep silent from the mystical things, but also from the ethical things; for in every place in which it was necessary to stand and be established and to be ready for a listening, a fall has occurred, and everywhere I cast down silence. Therefore, the sticking of the tongue to the [palate] signifies silence.

...the larynx. "If I forget you, Jerusalem, let my tongue cling to my larynx, if I do not remember you" (Psalm 137:1). If I do not remember you (Psalm 102:3), let me take silence. 16 And you have led me into the dust of death. Even if the voice were in the presence of Jesus, even if it were in the presence of the holy men who knew [God], having become like the wicked in the place of affliction, having been humbled—"you humbled us in a place of affliction" (Psalm 102:3). For the ones saying [this] are holy, as the conjunction signifies of the psalm. "Body of death" (Psalm 49:14) is said of that which surrounds us, and it is also said "dust of death" (Psalm 49:14). It is not "dust of death" in essence, but because those being forced from the life outside the body come into this, the body is named death. "Into the dust" therefore "of death you have led me" (Psalm 49:14). If it were life, it would have been led upward; for to be led up is to be brought into life and blessedness and an immortal state. Even if the Savior therefore says this, this: the light "into the dust of death you have led me" (Psalm 49:14). They descended into a body so that I might die on behalf of all, so that "by the grace of God above all" (1 Cor 15:10) I might taste "death."

Differently, therefore, from other men, it is said "dust of death" and "body of death" for the Savior; for if the body becomes death when the one using it sins, and Jesus did not sin, he came into the dust of death being able to undergo death. Therefore, those who stumble, saying that he is either merely a man or a heavenly body having endured [nothing], and attributing death to him, are mistaken. It is not so. Divinity, without such a thing, does not undergo death; for it is immortality. And just as for God, being light according to truth and essence, this is not darkness to him, so also in life there is no death. It is impossible for life to receive death. But he took upon himself something capable of undergoing death and division, and this is called death essential to it; for many other things are said of some things as not being essential to them, such as "garment, my footwear." In this way, the body is not essential. If, therefore, he says life receives death, he says receiving according to the outside. And I will say something paradoxical: just as the body receives death, so life vivifies the body. And this common life, the entanglement of the soul with the body, provides the vital movements to the body. How much more then, life itself or the...

title: The Dogs and the Assembly of Fornicators
english: A soul having been made alive by the preceding and blessed life; and it is good also to say: 'You have led me into the dust of death' (Ps 22:14). It was not He who descended into the dust of death, nor did the soul descend into the dust of death. But this happens to those being incarnated through wickedness.

Since He himself, for the sake of the economy and the salvation of all, received a body and God prepared a body for Him, He says: 'to be led by God into the dust of death.' But when men were, who confessing say: 'our belly has been joined to the earth' (Ps 79:10). When anyone does not nourish himself with the heavenly breads, the heavenly food, but the earthly—not the earthly sensible, but the opposite of the true bread—this food binds the soul being nourished to the matter, and it becomes a humiliation into the dust of the soul.

Here, however, the soul was not humiliated by Jesus into the dust, but was led by God. He came to this in an economical manner; for He had by no means committed sin, even though He was receptive; for if he were not receptive, he would not be praised at all. The abstaining therefore from sins brings praise to the one who has refrained when he was by nature prone to act.

Now, is dust and death the same thing? No; for He did not say: 'and into the dust of death You have led me.' If dust and death were the same, He would have said: 'into the dust of death You have led me'; but: 'into the dust of death.' The mortal body, which is able to be dissolved from the essence carrying it, is 'the dust of death.' And perhaps also by a second sense it is the dust of death, because it brings death to the flesh-loving soul.

'Many dogs have surrounded me; the body of the saints is dead'—for 'always they carry the death of Jesus in the body' (2 Cor 4:10). But the dead body does not have desires; for how is it possible? Is the mortal living? And it lives then when it is entwined with the soul. Then it has desires. Having died, it does not have desires. Having killed the members which are on the earth, it does not have desire.

Now, is the soul found to be the cause of sin? The soul of the one sinning is the cause of the sin; for nothing else is sin except the disobedience of a commandment, the transgression of a law. The body is not under a commandment in order that it might also transgress. The soul, transgressing, leads the body into...

To serve the sinful eyes; it is like an instrument. We do not say that the sword that sheds blood is a killer, but rather the one using it? For how is it possible? If we do not attribute sin or righteousness to a rational animal having a soul, do we attribute these things to the soulless body? By its own logic, the body is soulless.

'For many dogs have surrounded me, a company of fornicators has enclosed me, they have gripped my hands and my feet' (Psalm 22:17). Thus write: 'For many dogs have surrounded me, a company of fornicators has enclosed me,' because of this 'they have gripped my hands and my feet.' The 'for' is a causal conjunction. It is not attached to those following: 'You have led me into the pit of death,' 'for many dogs have surrounded me.' No, but: since 'many dogs have surrounded me and a company of fornicators has enclosed me,' because of this 'they have gripped my hands and my feet.' Humans remaining would not have done this.

But he says 'dogs' here to mean men having a dog-like manner. And he slanders the movements of the dog in many ways. They are entirely base toward filth. Thus, it has become customary to call the lawless and the women 'dogs' in this sense. Indeed, even the law also, suggesting this meaning, counted the dog along with the prostitute: 'You shall not substitute a dog for a change, nor a prostitute's hire' (Deuteronomy 23:18). He did not say a change of a donkey or a horse; for these changes were being brought into the house of the Lord.

And it is both shameless—'and the dogs are shameless to the soul'—and flattering. Therefore, men who have such movements are called dogs in judgment. These, then, surrounded the Savior. When they were sheep of God, they were at least outside the dog-like state. But when the people had become lost sheep, the loss did not turn them into non-existence, but into a dog-like, deficient, and scorpion-like state. And all this was said regarding the Hebrews: 'And all dogs are inward, knowing how to bark' (Psalm 22:16).

When the Israelites thought against the Savior, then they became dogs. And the being a 'company of fornicators' followed their becoming dogs; for when they were sheep, they were a divine flock. So they became dogs around me and a company of fornicators. Because of this they cast me to the cross; for the...
